apps.name: Code reviewer
apps.description: Reads a diff the way a senior reviewer does, and says what would break.
apps.readme:
# Code reviewer — a demo bundle for the ADI Store

An agent that reads a diff the way a senior engineer does: what would break, which line, and then
it stops.

**It is here to be read as much as to be run.** This is the smallest thing a marketplace item can
be — one agent and nothing else — so it is the file to copy when you want to publish one of your
own. Install it with a click from [the ADI Store](https://withadi.dev/store/reviewer), or:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install store/reviewer
```

## What makes this a bundle

Nothing but the directory it is in. A marketplace item is a git repository whose top level holds
one directory per *kind* of element, and this one holds `agents/`:

```text
agents/
  reviewer.toml     # one agent, named by its filename
```

The eight kinds are `agents/`, `tools/`, `dashboards/`, `llm/`, `embeddings/`, `services/`,
`triggers/` and `project/`. A repository may carry any of them; the installer reads what is
actually there rather than trusting the manifest, and an element can be installed on its own:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install store/reviewer/agents/reviewer
```

## What is in the agent

`reviewer.toml` is an ordinary agent definition — the same file `adi-mono agents save` writes:

- `backend = "harness:adi"` — the loop it runs in.
- `system_prompt` — the whole of what makes it a reviewer rather than a chat.
- `[[secrets]]` — it declares `REVIEWER_GITHUB_TOKEN`. **Declaring is not having**: the install
  lands the agent with the secret named and unset, and the panel says so on the row. Nothing is
  read from your machine and nothing is filled in for you.

## Publishing one of your own

1. Put your elements in kind directories at the root of a repository, as above.
2. Push it, and take the commit: `git rev-parse HEAD`.
3. Add an entry to a marketplace manifest naming that repository and that **full 40-hex commit**.
   The pin is the point: what somebody read is what installs, and moving onto a newer commit is
   `marketplace update`, an act they take.

The format, and every rule the installer enforces, is in
[`docs/marketplace.md`](https://github.com/adi-family/mono/blob/main/docs/marketplace.md).

## What it does not do

Nothing runs on arrival. An installed agent is a definition on your disk until you run it, and
this one has no trigger, no service and no schedule — there is nothing here that starts itself.

apps.name: Changelog tools
apps.description: Turn a range of commits into release notes, and refuse a subject nobody can read.
apps.readme:
# Changelog tools — a demo bundle for the ADI Store

Two small tools an agent can reach for: one turns a commit range into release notes, the other
refuses a commit subject nobody will be able to read in a year.

**It is here to be read as much as to be run.** It is the example of a bundle that carries *tools*
and nothing else, and of the smallest useful thing a tool can be — a shell script with a comment
at the top. Install it with a click from [the ADI Store](https://withadi.dev/store/changelog-tools),
or:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install store/changelog-tools
```

## What makes this a bundle

The directory names at the top level, and nothing else:

```text
tools/
  changelog.sh      # one tool, named by its filename
  commit-lint.sh    # and another
```

A tool is a file an agent may run. It arrives as a tool in your store — readable, editable, and
yours — and an agent only reaches it when its own definition lists it (`bin_tools`). Installing a
tool gives it to nobody by itself.

Either one installs on its own:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install store/changelog-tools/tools/changelog
```

## What is in them

`changelog.sh` is five lines of `git log`. `commit-lint.sh` is a regex and an exit code. That is
deliberate: a tool is not a program you maintain, it is the shortest thing that answers one
question, and it is worth publishing exactly when the shortest thing is still not obvious.

## Publishing one of your own

1. Put your elements in kind directories at the root of a repository, as above.
2. Push it, and take the commit: `git rev-parse HEAD`.
3. Add an entry to a marketplace manifest naming that repository and that **full 40-hex commit**.

The format is in
[`docs/marketplace.md`](https://github.com/adi-family/mono/blob/main/docs/marketplace.md).

## What it does not do

Nothing here runs on arrival, and nothing here reaches the network. Both scripts read a git
repository you point them at and print to stdout.

apps.name: Standup board
apps.description: What every agent finished yesterday, on one screen.
apps.readme:
# Standup board — a demo bundle for the ADI Store

One screen that answers the only question a standup ever asks: what moved since yesterday. Every
agent that finished a run in the last day gets a line — what it was asked for, what it shipped, and
how long it took.

**It is here to be read as much as to be run.** It is the example of a bundle that carries a
*dashboard*: a frontend and a backend that ADI serves for you, on a hostname of their own. Install
it with a click from [the ADI Store](https://withadi.dev/store/standup), or:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install store/standup
```

## What makes this a bundle

```text
dashboards/
  standup/
    frontend/
      index.html          # the shell ADI keeps up to date for you
      index.ts            # the entry point, also generated and kept current
      modules/standup.ts  # YOUR code — migration never touches this
    backend/
      index.ts            # the entry point
      routes/standup.ts   # YOUR code
```

The split matters and is the one thing to copy: **`modules/` and `routes/` are yours**, and the
three entry points are ADI's — it rewrites them in place when its own templates move on, which is
how a shell fix reaches dashboards that already exist. An installed dashboard marks them
`--skip-worktree`, so `git status` in your copy shows only your own work.

## What it does not do

It reads the runs your machine already has. It writes nothing, it has no settings, and it reaches
no network. And **installed is not started**: it arrives inert, on a hostname reserved but not
served, until you press Start — the panel's Dashboards page, or `adi-mono marketplace start
<id>`.

## Publishing one of your own

1. `adi-mono dashboards create <name>`, write your panel in `modules/` and your routes in
   `routes/`.
2. Push the dashboard's directory as `dashboards/<name>/…` at the root of a repository — without
   `config.toml`, `.adi/` or `node_modules/`, which belong to the installing machine.
3. Take the commit (`git rev-parse HEAD`) and add an entry to a marketplace manifest naming that
   repository and that **full 40-hex commit**.

The rules are in
[`docs/marketplace.md`](https://github.com/adi-family/mono/blob/main/docs/marketplace.md); how to
write the dashboard itself is in
[`guides/dashboards.md`](https://github.com/adi-family/mono/blob/main/guides/dashboards.md).

apps.name: CRM suite
apps.description: A follow-up agent, its import tool, the backend it answers on, and the board that watches both.
apps.readme:
# CRM suite — a demo bundle for the ADI Store

Four pieces of one habit, published together: an agent that drafts the follow-up nobody got round
to sending, the tool that loads your contacts, the model backend it answers on, and the board that
shows who has gone quiet.

**It is here to be read as much as to be run.** It is the example of a bundle that carries *more
than one kind* — which is what a bundle is for, and what the other demos deliberately do not show.
Install it with a click from [the ADI Store](https://withadi.dev/store/crm-suite), or:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install store/crm-suite
```

## What makes this a bundle

Four kind directories at the top level, and every element named by its own filename:

```text
agents/sales-bot.toml        # drafts the message
tools/csv-import.sh          # loads a contacts export
llm/gpt5.toml                # the backend sales-bot answers on
dashboards/crm/…             # the board that watches both
```

**Each of them installs on its own**, which is the other half of what a bundle means — take the
tool without the agent, or the dashboard without either:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install store/crm-suite/tools/csv-import
```

The agent names `csv-import` in its `bin_tools`, so installing the agent alone leaves it with an
empty bin until the tool lands too. That is the ordinary state of an agent whose tools are not
ticked, not an error.

## Where it goes

Installing asks: a project of its own (recommended — it keeps these four in one place), a project
you already have, or globally. A bundle of four elements is exactly the case a project is for.

## What it does not do

`llm/gpt5.toml` names `OPENAI_API_KEY`; it does not carry one and nothing reads yours. The agent
runs when you run it, the dashboard serves when you start it, and the tool runs when something
calls it.

## Publishing one of your own

1. Put each element in its kind directory at the root of a repository, as above.
2. Push it, and take the commit: `git rev-parse HEAD`.
3. Add an entry to a marketplace manifest naming that repository and that **full 40-hex commit**.
   `elements` in the entry is a *preview* for the listing — what actually installs is read off the
   pinned commit's own tree.

The format is in
[`docs/marketplace.md`](https://github.com/adi-family/mono/blob/main/docs/marketplace.md).
